p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: George Pickett sat on his horse and watched his division come back.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: They came in clusters and straggles, the survivors of a mile-wide charge across open ground under artillery and musketry. Some walked steadily. Some stumbled. Some were helping others walk. All of them had the look of men who had been through something that no words could explain.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Of the three brigades Pickett had sent forward — Garnett, Kemper, Armistead — Garnett was dead, Kemper was critically wounded and briefly a prisoner, Armistead was dying beyond the stone wall he had crossed. The division had suffered nearly 2,700 casualties from 5,500 engaged. Forty-nine percent.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Lee rode forward to meet them.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He rode along the broken line, and he said to them, over and over, the same thing: 'It is all my fault. It is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Pickett came to Lee. Lee told him to reform his division — there might be a Union counterattack coming.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Pickett looked at Lee. 'General Lee,' he said, 'I have no division.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Lee never acknowledged, officially or privately, that ordering the charge had been a mistake. He praised the courage of his men and said that more support should have been provided. In his official report he blamed himself in the most general terms.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Pickett blamed Lee specifically. For the rest of his life he told anyone who would listen that Lee had destroyed his division. When someone praised Lee in Pickett's presence years after the war, Pickett said quietly: 'That man destroyed my division.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He said it with the measured tone of a man who had been carrying the weight of it for decades.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: George Armstrong Custer was twenty-three years old and had been a brigadier general for exactly eight days.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 1 of 12

p: He had earned the promotion through a combination of extraordinary courage and extraordinary luck — the kind of officer who seemed to attract bullets that always missed. He wore a custom uniform of black velvet with gold trim that made him conspicuous on any battlefield. He wore his hair in long golden ringlets. He was, in the Army of the Potomac, impossible to ignore.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 2 of 12

p: On the afternoon of July 3, while Pickett's infantry was crossing the open fields toward Cemetery Ridge, Stuart's cavalry moved east of Gettysburg to sweep around the Union rear. If Stuart could strike the Union rear simultaneously with the infantry assault on the front, the Army of the Potomac might be destroyed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 3 of 12

p: Gregg's cavalry division blocked the road. Custer's Michigan Brigade — 1,900 troopers on fresh horses — was the striking force.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 4 of 12

p: Stuart advanced. Hampton's South Carolinians and Fitz Lee's Virginians moved forward in what Confederate veterans later described as a magnificent charge — thousands of horsemen covering the ground in a sweeping wall of cavalry.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 5 of 12
